title: Redwood Private VPC security architecture deep dive with Pinnacle Finance
summary: Deep dive covering Redwood Private (VPC) security architecture: network isolation patterns, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, VPC endpoints/PrivateLink, bastion/elevated access patterns, encryption and BYOK with KMS/HSM, audit logging retention and SIEM integration, RBAC/SSO/SCIM provisioning, SOC2/ISO artifacts. Agreed next steps: share SOC2/ISO docs, provide detailed network diagram for pilot, schedule follow-up architecture workshop and pilot kick-off.

Elena to produce initial private VPC network diagram and recommended firewall rules by 2026-03-20
Schedule 90-minute architecture workshop with Pinnacle infra + security teams week of 2026-03-23
Provide pilot quote and draft SOW for private deployment by 2026-03-24

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-15
Time: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Elena Park (Redwood SE), Marcus Li (Redwood Security Eng); Jenna Morales (Pinnacle CISO), Tom Becker (VP Eng), Priya Shah (Cloud Architect)

Summary: quick sync to walk through architecture requirements for a Private/VPC deployment; heavy focus on network isolation, ingress/egress firewalling, and encryption/BYOK requirements for regulated data.

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick roll call?
[00:12] Jenna: Jenna here, hi.
[00:15] Tom: Tom on my side.
[00:17] Priya: Priya, Cloud architect.
[00:20] Samir: Great, Elena and Marcus from our side are going to walk through the private VPC design. We're focused on the security controls you asked about in the RFP — SOC2, KMS, network isolation, egress controls.
[00:38] Elena: Okay jumping in, we've got a couple of patterns we recommend. First, full network isolation using dedicated VPC with private subnets only for inference nodes, management plane in a separate control VPC, and VPC peering or Transit Gateway for control-plane access. For Pinnacle we typically recommend no public IPs on inference hosts, NAT for controlled egress, and explicit VPC endpoints for S3 and other AWS services.
[01:12] Priya: Quick question, when you say control plane in separate VPC, do you need any inbound from internet to that control plane? Our security team likes to limit exposure.
[01:25] Marcus: Good question. The control plane can be customer-managed in Private mode; Redwood also offers a control-plane connector that runs as an outbound-only tunnel. For our private deployment we can operate via mTLS mutual-authenticated outbound connections from your VPC to our control plane, so no inbound firewall rules are required on your side.
[01:52] Tom: So that would be egress-only from our VPC — that helps a lot. Is it port locked?
[01:59] Elena: Yes, we restrict to a small set of destination IPs and TLS ports, and recommend using a gateway or proxy in your egress path to centralize allowlists. We provide a list of IPs and DNS names for the control plane endpoints.
[02:20] Jenna: On compliance: we need SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 evidence. Are those available for the Private deployment?
[02:29] Samir: Yes, we can share our SOC2 and ISO27001 reports under an NDA; they'll be the same baseline artifacts. For Private deployments we augment with deployment-specific attestations and a runbook that documents encryption, access controls and logging configuration.
[02:48] Priya: About keys — we have a BYOK requirement. Can Redwood integrate with our KMS/HSM?
[02:56] Marcus: Absolutely. We support BYOK via customer-managed KMS keys — either AWS KMS or a customer HSM. The private runtime uses those keys for model artifact encryption at rest and for EBS/S3 encryption. We also support KMS envelope encryption and rotation policies. We'll provide an integration checklist with IAM policy examples.
[03:20] Tom: Do you store any keys on Redwood side?
[03:23] Marcus: No, with BYOK we don't have plaintext keys; Redwood only sees encrypted material. For HSM flows we can use a proxy that performs crypto ops in your HSM and returns signed tokens.
[03:36] Elena: Also, note we support both envelope encryption and client-side encryption for the most sensitive workflows.
[03:45] Priya: How about audit logs? We need 7 years for some records and SIEM integration to Splunk.
[03:53] Elena: We emit detailed audit logs: API requests, audit trail for model versions, admin RBAC changes, and control-plane actions. For Private, logs can be forwarded to your CloudWatch / Splunk via a secure forwarder or to a Syslog endpoint. Retention is configurable; we can export to S3 with lifecycle policies.
[04:15] Jenna: Are those logs tamper-evident? We need integrity guarantees.
[04:20] Marcus: We support write-once S3 with object lock for tamper resistance and can timestamp log batches. We also provide signed log digests to support integrity verification.
[04:33] Tom: Networking — firewalling specifics: security groups, NACLs, stateful vs stateless — any recommendations?
[04:41] Elena: Security groups for host-level, stateful, tightly scoped egress/inbound rules. NACLs as an additional layer per subnet for defense-in-depth. For egress we suggest an egress proxy with allowlist and TLS inspection at the proxy boundary if you do deep packet inspection.
[05:00] Priya: We use strict NACL deny policies for any unexpected ports. Will that break the platform?
[05:06] Elena: Not if you open the small set of required egress destinations and ports; we'll provide those. Also, for manageability we recommend using a NAT gateway plus Route Tables and VPC endpoints for AWS services so you don't need broad internet egress from inference subnets.
[05:26] Jenna: What about PrivateLink? We need to avoid cross-account peering if possible.
[05:32] Marcus: We support AWS PrivateLink endpoints — we can publish service endpoints into your account so traffic never traverses the public internet. That also simplifies firewall rules; you just allow the endpoint.
[05:45] Tom: For on-prem installations — we have a co-lo — what changes?
[05:49] Elena: On-prem is similar conceptually: private networks, no public IPs on inference boxes, and a bastion jump host for admin. For control-plane connectivity we can use an outbound-only tunnel over TLS to a control plane aggregator, or you can run the control plane locally in air-gapped mode.
[06:10] Priya: If we are air-gapped, will we lose telemetry and updates?
[06:14] Marcus: You'll run a local control plane and we provide an offline update process. Telemetry can be pushed to your SIEM on-prem. It's more operationally heavy, but supported.
[06:25] Jenna: RBAC and SSO — we run Okta and expect SCIM user provisioning and SAML SSO.
[06:34] Elena: We support SAML 2.0 for SSO and SCIM for provisioning. We map IdP groups to RBAC roles in Redwood Console. For Private we can integrate with your IdP via IdP endpoints inside the VPC or via secure connectors; SCIM provisioning can be automated.
[06:56] Priya: Can we enforce least privilege so that only certain teams can deploy models or pull logs?
[07:01] Marcus: Yes, roles can be scoped to model namespaces, environment tags, and actions. We enforce audit logging on role changes. Also support MFA enforced via your IdP.
[07:12] Tom: Any concerns about latency with PrivateLink or NAT vs public endpoints for embeddings endpoints?
[07:20] Elena: PrivateLink adds minimal latency — usually <5ms in-region. NAT and egress via a central proxy can add some tail latency depending on architecture. For strict latency SLAs we recommend colocating inference in the same AZ and using VPC endpoints or PrivateLink rather than hairpinning through central proxies.
[07:44] Jenna: We have data residency constraints; some datasets must remain in-region. How does Redwood ensure region residency for models and artifacts?
[07:53] Marcus: You can pin model storage and inference pools to specific regions and we won't replicate cross-region unless explicitly configured. We persist artifacts in region-specific S3 buckets with region ACLs.
[08:07] Priya: For encryption in transit are you doing mutual TLS between components?
[08:12] Elena: Yes, mTLS inside the cluster for node-to-node and control-plane communication. Client boundaries use TLS with strong ciphers and we can require client certs for admin APIs.
[08:25] Tom: How are secrets handled on the hosts — do you use kernel keyrings, Vault, or something else?
[08:31] Marcus: We integrate with HashiCorp Vault or cloud KMS for secrets. For ephemeral secrets we use instance metadata only for bootstrapping and then fetch short-lived tokens from Vault. We avoid long-lived secrets on disk.
[08:45] Jenna: For proof to auditor — can you produce architecture diagrams, control matrices, and a runbook for how keys are rotated and how audit logs are stored?
[08:54] Samir: Yes, that's part of the package we deliver for enterprise pilots. We'll produce an architecture diagram, mapping to SOC2 controls, an ops runbook, and example policies.
[09:07] Priya: Network egress filtering — we need to block DNS exfiltration. Do you have guidance?
[09:13] Elena: Use a DNS proxy or resolver inside the VPC that enforces allowlists. Combine with egress proxy and deep packet inspection. Additionally, monitor for anomalous DNS queries in logs.
[09:28] Tom: On firewalling, do you recommend host-based firewalls as well?
[09:32] Marcus: Host-level firewalls (iptables/nftables) are a good extra layer; our deployment images include a hardened baseline you can enable. For strict compliance, we recommend host hardening plus container runtime restrictions.
[09:47] Jenna: Are there any non-negotiable ports or protocols we need to open?
[09:51] Elena: Only a small set: TLS (443) outbound to control plane endpoints, KMS endpoints (region-specific), and any VPC endpoint traffic. We'll supply the exact list.
[09:59] Tom: Regarding Egress through corporate proxy — some of our infra teams require all egress through a central proxy with TLS intercept. Will that break mTLS?
[10:08] Marcus: If the proxy performs TLS MITM, it will break mTLS. For such environments we recommend a proxy that supports TCP tunnel passthrough for the control-plane connections or use PrivateLink endpoints to avoid proxy interception.
[10:25] Priya: For data at rest — you mentioned S3 and EBS encryption. Are snapshots encrypted?
[10:31] Elena: Yes, snapshots are encrypted with KMS. With BYOK we ensure the same KMS keys apply to ephemeral volumes and snapshots so customer controls key rotation.
[10:42] Jenna: How do you handle access to model artifacts? Who can pull weights?
[10:47] Marcus: Artifact access is RBAC-controlled; we log every artifact pull and support tokenized short-lived access. Artifact stores are in your account for Private deployments when required.
[11:00] Tom: Incident response — what is Redwood's role vs customer?
[11:06] Samir: For Private deployments, incident response is collaborative. Redwood provides runbooks and assists with triage; your security team owns network perimeter controls and log access. For Dedicated/Hosted we have more responsibility and an on-call playbook.
[11:21] Priya: Can we run vulnerability scans on the images and the runtime?
[11:25] Elena: Yes, we publish image SBOMs and allow you to run scans; we also run internal scanning and publish CVE reports for known components.
[11:36] Tom: Any guidance on firewall rules for cross-account S3 access used by the artifacts?
[11:42] Marcus: Use VPC endpoints and bucket policies tied to VPC endpoint IDs or IAM roles. That way you don't need public S3 access.
[11:53] Jenna: For long-term retention of logs — if we export to Glacier for compliance is that supported?
[11:58] Elena: Yes, we can export audit logs to a dedicated S3 bucket and lifecycle to Glacier or archive tiers.
[12:08] Samir: I'm going to summarize and make sure we've captured action items — Elena will produce the network diagram and firewall rule set, Marcus will produce the KMS/BYOK and HSM checklist, and I'll send SOC2/ISO reports. Then we'll schedule a 90-minute workshop.
[12:25] Priya: One operational question — how do we rotate credentials for the admin users?
[12:30] Marcus: We recommend IdP-driven provisioning with SCIM and enforce periodic rotation via IdP policies; if you use local accounts we support automated rotation via Vault.
[12:42] Tom: About telemetry — do you collect PII in logs? We prefer obfuscation.
[12:48] Elena: We do not intentionally log PII; we can redact sensitive fields and provide filtering rules before forwarding logs to your SIEM.
[13:00] Jenna: Any performance impact from encryption at rest or mTLS?
[13:05] Marcus: Minimal — envelope encryption and KMS calls add a small CPU overhead on boot and a negligible per-request overhead for metadata operations. mTLS adds handshake cost but again small if you reuse connections and kv caches. In our benchmarks for similar banks we saw <1-2% throughput overhead.
[13:26] Priya: For high throughput inference we sometimes need to pin instances and avoid autoscale — any security tradeoffs there?
[13:32] Elena: Pinning instances is fine; just ensure you have long-lived key handling and periodic rekeying; autoscale adds complexity for ephemeral keys but is compatible with short-lived tokens.
[13:45] Tom: Are there SLAs around patching?
[13:49] Samir: For Private customers we recommend a shared patching cadence; Redwood will publish CVE patches and we can agree on maintenance windows in the SOW.
[14:02] Jenna: For the architecture diagram, can you also show data flow for model downloads, infer request, and logging path?
[14:09] Elena: Yes, the diagram will include control-plane flows, artifact staging, inference path, and log export.
[14:18] Tom: Any gotchas with using KMS cross-account keys? We might want the ops account to own keys.
[14:24] Marcus: Cross-account KMS is supported; you just need IAM policies and grants configured. We'll include example policies.
[14:33] Priya: For the audit logs we want immutability and a hash chain if possible. You mentioned signed log digests — can you explain?
[14:40] Marcus: We compute a daily digest of log batches, sign the digest with a key, and store it in a tamper-evident bucket. That allows you to validate the integrity of a day's logs.
[14:55] Jenna: On the legal side — we'll need data processing addenda and DPA updates for the pilot.
[15:02] Samir: We'll route that to legal and include in the SOW.
[15:08] Tom: Okay this is super helpful. Can you also include a short checklist of minimal firewall rules to get the pilot running?
[15:15] Elena: Yes, that'll be part of the network diagram pack. Minimal list: allow outbound TLS to control-plane endpoints, allow VPC endpoint traffic to S3/KMS, permit internal mTLS ports between nodes, and block all other inbound to inference subnets.
[15:34] Priya: Timeline: we're aiming to start pilot in April. Is that feasible?
[15:38] Samir: Yes, if we get the SOW signed and network access arranged we can kick off in early April.
[15:45] Jenna: Anything else on compliance — encryption algorithms or key lengths?
[15:49] Marcus: We recommend AES-256 for data at rest and TLS 1.2+ with ECDHE ciphers for transport. KMS keys should be RSA-2048 or ECC P-256 depending on HSM.
[16:05] Tom: For monitoring, do you ship prometheus metrics or do we scrape?
[16:09] Elena: We export Prometheus-format metrics and also provide a metrics push option; for Private you can scrape from a secured endpoint. We'll provide auth tokens or mTLS certs for scrapes.
[16:22] Priya: Any recommended rate limits on API calls to avoid noisy neighbors in our infra?
[16:27] Elena: We'll recommend per-model and per-namespace throttles; for pilot we'll size capacity and set quotas.
[16:36] Samir: Great — I think we have the items we need. We'll share the docs and set the architecture workshop. Any final questions?
[16:45] Jenna: Not from me, thanks.
[16:47] Tom: None here.
[16:49] Priya: All good.
[16:51] Samir: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up on the action items and send invites for the workshop. Bye.

Notes: Transcript contains typical pauses, small transcription artefacts and occasional speaker overlap. References made to inbound/outbound tunnel, PrivateLink, NAT, VPC endpoints, KMS, HSM, SCIM, SAML, SOC2/ISO.
